mstts:express-as.prosody: As we wrap up our journey through “A Problem from Hell,” it’s clear that the story of genocide isn’t just about faraway places or nameless faces. It’s about the choices people make behind closed doors, the courage to speak up, and that constant push and pull between what we know is right, and what actually happens. There aren’t any simple answers here, but there are a few truths that really stand out. First, calling something by its name is just the beginning—real change comes when we act on what we know. So often, politics and fear get in the way of doing what’s right. And while the voices of survivors and witnesses matter deeply, sometimes, even that isn’t enough to move the needle. But here’s something powerful: small acts of advocacy—no matter how tiny they seem—can make a difference, even when the world’s big systems resist. The fight to stop genocide never really ends. It asks for constant awareness, and real courage. Maybe it’s easy to feel like nothing you do will matter, faced with tragedies this big. But history reminds us that change, even if it’s slow, really is possible. Yes, there have been failures—but there have been moments of real bravery and compassion, too. If you’ve ever wondered, “Does it matter if I notice, or care, or speak up?”—remember: every time you pay attention, every time you refuse to turn away, you’re helping shape a better future. The struggle against indifference isn’t over, and the responsibility to care belongs to each of us. Even if the world seems unmoved, your voice, your witness, your willingness to take action—these are the things that can help bend the arc of history toward justice. So as you move forward, remember: you’re not powerless. Every small act counts.
